rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to survey retention and reveal critical peak pairs across the unknown mixture. The high final organic fraction and remaining hold time favor observing all 10 compounds within 42 minutes.

All peaks are comfortably resolved, so double the gradient slope to reduce the time penalty. Keeping temperature and endpoints unchanged will isolate how gradient compression affects the critical separations.

Test an intermediate gradient duration to recover the compressed central separations while retaining much of the time savings. This brackets the resolution–time tradeoff before adjusting temperature or starting composition.

Keep the near-optimal gradient and increase temperature by 5 °C to test selectivity for the sole unresolved pair. This may raise its resolution above 1.5 while keeping the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

The critical pair converged as temperature rose to 45 °C; testing 55 °C may separate it again after an elution-order reversal. Higher temperature should also preserve the zero time penalty, while the full table will reveal any new critical pair.

Increase temperature to improve the remaining critical separation, while using a shallower gradient to protect the earlier pair that narrowed at 55 °C. The last peak is expected to remain near the zero-time-penalty window.

Return to 55 °C and slightly steepen the gradient, which may improve the near-threshold pair following its temperature-induced order reversal. The earlier pair has some resolution margin at this temperature, and the shorter gradient should retain zero time penalty.

Test a slightly shallower gradient between injections 5 and 7, aiming to retain CRF 1.000 while improving the earlier critical pair. The later critical pair is expected to remain just above 1.5, with no time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a higher starting organic fraction to seek another maximum-score method with greater resolution margin. This probes starting-composition selectivity while retaining the successful temperature and gradient duration.

Lengthen injection 9’s gradient to recover resolution of the earlier critical pair while retaining the later pair’s improved separation. This may provide another maximum-score method with more balanced resolution margins and no time penalty.

Extend the successful trend of increasing starting organic fraction and gradient duration to seek greater critical-pair resolution margins. This method is expected to keep the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window while potentially retaining CRF 1.000.

Slightly lengthen injection 11’s gradient to bring the earlier critical pair above 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s margin. The last peak is projected near 9.4 minutes, potentially retaining zero time penalty and achieving CRF 1.000.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope from injection 12 to probe the neighborhood of its balanced critical-pair resolutions. This should retain adequate separation while placing the last peak just below the apparent 10-minute time-penalty threshold.

Test a neighboring method between the successful starting-composition and gradient-duration settings. Relative to injection 10, the longer gradient should strengthen the earlier critical separation while potentially retaining sufficient later-pair resolution and zero time penalty.

Test a gradient slope between injections 10 and 14, both of which achieved the maximum CRF. This should preserve baseline separation and zero time penalty while mapping the range of maximum-score methods.

Use a slope between injections 11 and 12 to recover the earlier critical separation while preserving the later pair’s margin. This is a promising shorter alternative to injection 12 that may also achieve the maximum CRF.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore a lower-temperature alternative to the narrow high-temperature optimum. Cooling relative to injection 3 may improve its central critical pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes, though adjacent separations must be checked.

Test a gradient slope close to injection 12, which achieved CRF 1.000 with balanced critical-pair resolutions near 1.70. The lower endpoint should still exceed the composition at which the last peak elutes, potentially preserving maximum performance with a shorter programmed gradient.

Use nearly the same gradient slope as injection 12 but end at a lower organic fraction after 10 minutes. All peaks are expected to elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, potentially preserving CRF 1.000 with a shorter programmed gradient and lower final organic content.

Preserve injection 7’s gradient slope and temperature while shortening the programmed gradient to 8 minutes. Because its last peak eluted before this gradient would end at the outlet, this method is expected to retain CRF 1.000 with a lower final organic fraction.

Keep the gradient slope and temperature of injections 7 and 20, which both achieved the maximum CRF. This intermediate endpoint should reproduce their separation because all compounds elute before the gradient reaches its final composition.

Preserve injection 18’s successful slope but begin the final hold before the last peak elutes. This tests whether a lower final organic fraction can retain complete elution below 10 minutes and CRF 1.000 without disturbing the earlier critical separations.

Retain injection 7’s successful slope through all early separations, then hold at 50% organic. This tests whether the faster maximum-score method can also use a lower endpoint while keeping the last peak below the time-penalty threshold.

Test a slope between injections 9 and 10 to seek a slightly faster maximum-score method at 10% starting organic. The 60% endpoint should allow the last peak to elute during the gradient while both critical pairs are predicted to remain above 1.5.

Slightly steepen injection 24’s gradient to seek a shorter maximum-score method with balanced critical-pair resolutions. Interpolation predicts both critical resolutions near 1.6 and the last peak near 7.8 minutes, retaining zero time penalty.
